title: Shadow Rollforward and Mesh Simulation Playbook
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview and purpose:

This playbook documents the Shadow Rollforward and Mesh Simulation pattern: a structured, low-risk pathway for validating model upgrades, quantized variants, and routing policy changes using a combination of shadow traffic, synthetic mesh simulations, and progressive rollforward rules. It complements the standard canary/cutover runbooks by emphasizing reproducible simulation meshes, cost-sensitive quant variants, and automated failure classification to shorten time-to-safe-promotion.

Who should use this:
- ML engineers preparing model promotions from staging to production
- SRE and platform engineers owning rollout automation and routing policies
- Applied ML / evaluation teams designing eval harness integrations

Scope and constraints:
- Applies to text generation, chat, and embedding routes that support shadow mirroring and model variant routing.
- Not intended for datasets that contain regulated PII unless Private deployment controls are in place.
- Requires the evaluation harness to be able to replay requests deterministically (see Pre-reqs).

Definitions:
- Shadow Rollforward: Gradual promotion path where new model variants receive mirrored traffic and simulated production meshes before taking live traffic.
- Mesh Simulation: Orchestrated synthetic traffic generator that reshapes request distributions (context lengths, few-shot examples, system prompts) to emulate production slices.

Prerequisites:
1) Promotion artifacts:
   - Signed model bundle (model-id, sha256, quant-profile) stored in model registry.
   - Evaluation report with slice-level metrics and accepted thresholds.
2) Platform capabilities:
   - Shadow mirroring enabled at route level and/or request proxy.
   - Canary and rollout policy engine accessible (canary weight scheduling, automatic rollback hooks).
   - Evaluation harness with seedable RNG and replay mode.
3) Observability:
   - Per-route token-level latency and cost tracking in Redwood Console.
   - Quality monitors (ROUGE/BLEU approximations, semantic similarity, hallucination detectors) hooked into alerting.

Key components in the pattern:
- Shadow router: duplicates production requests to candidate model(s) with adjustable sampling.
- Mesh simulator: synthesizes permutations of request context (prompt perturbation, prefix cache hit/miss simulation, dynamic shots).
- Quant variant manager: assigns quantization profile and GPU/backing variant used for experiments.
- Evaluator: aggregates shadow responses, computes metrics, and performs automatic regression classification (statistical and heuristic checks).

Acceptance criteria and SLOs (examples):
| Metric                             | Target (pass/fail)                       | Alert threshold | Action on breach |
|-----------------------------------|------------------------------------------|-----------------|------------------|
| Overall semantic similarity (avg) | >= 0.88 cosine to golden responses       | < 0.86          | Halt promotion   |
| Latency (p95, generation only)    | <= 450ms on dedicated tier               | > 600ms         | Revert variant   |
| Token cost delta                   | <= +12% vs baseline (same throughput)    | > +20%          | Investigate cost policy |
| Hallucination rate (slice top10)  | <= baseline + 1.5%                       | +2.5%           | Reject promotion |
| Stability index (answer churn)    | <= 0.05 increase                          | > 0.08          | Run deeper triage |

Note: Use slice-driven evaluation—measure per-customer, per-intent, and per-context-length buckets.

Mesh simulation design checklist:
- Identify 6–10 representative slices from production telemetry (e.g., helpdesk-paraphrase, code-completion, long-context summarization).
- For each slice, enumerate perturbations: template paraphrases, token masking, extra-system prompts, prefix cache warm/cold states.
- Define weightings to reflect production frequency and business criticality (weights must sum to 1).
- Add failure injections: truncated responses, partial KV-cache misses, and latency spikes to observe graceful degradation.

Procedure: Shadow Rollforward + Mesh Simulation (step-by-step)
1) Prepare artifacts and baseline: 
   - Lock baseline model version id and collect 24–72h telemetry for target routes.
   - Generate golden responses on a fixed seed set via eval harness.
2) Configure mesh: 
   - Create a mesh definition file that maps slices -> perturbations -> sample weights. See example below.
3) Deploy candidate model to a shadow-only endpoint (no live routing) with quant profiles set per the experiment.
4) Start shadow mirroring at 5% of production QPS. Mirror sampling should stratify by slice.
5) Run mesh simulation for N=12h or until the sample size per slice meets statistical power (min 500 examples per slice recommended).
6) Evaluate metrics using the evaluator; run both deterministic and stochastic checks (multi-seed aggregation).
7) Run regression classification: automatic triage should label any significant regressions into categories (semantic, latency/cost, instability, hallucination).
8) If pass, transition to progressive rollforward: 5% -> 20% -> 50% over successive windows with continuous shadowing of additional variants.
9) If fail, trigger fast rollback and automatic issue report creation with attached logs, sample traces, and a reproducible mesh replay spec.

Mesh definition example (YAML excerpt):

# mesh-definition.yaml
# top-level: slices with perturbations and weights
slices:
  - name: "support_paraphrase"
    weight: 0.28
    perturbations:
      - paraphrase_template: 10
      - add_system_prompt: 5
      - cold_kv_cache: 1
  - name: "long_context_summary"
    weight: 0.24
    perturbations:
      - truncate_context: 3
      - add_irrelevant_paragraph: 2
      - increased_shots: 1
  - name: "code_completion"
    weight: 0.12
    perturbations:
      - masked_tokens: 5
      - varying_indent: 1

Reproducible commands and snippets:
- Run mesh simulator (CLI):
  rwd-mesh simulate --mesh mesh-definition.yaml --samples 20000 --seed 42 --output ./mesh-results.json

- Start shadow mirroring (kubectl example for ingress config):
  kubectl patch configroute redwood-routing -p '{"spec": {"shadowPercent":5, "shadowTargets":[{"model":"candidate-v2","quant_profile":"q4_0"}]}}'

- Extract evaluator summary (python snippet):
  from rwd_eval import Aggregator
  agg = Aggregator('./mesh-results.json')
  report = agg.slice_summary(metrics=['cosine_sim','p95_latency','hallucination_rate'])
  print(report.to_markdown())

Failure classification and automated triage rules (examples):
- Rule A: If semantic similarity drops > 0.06 on any slice and p-value < 0.01 => label semantic_regression, priority P0.
- Rule B: If p95 latency increases > 30% and absolute p95 > 600ms => label perf_regression, throttle rollforward.
- Rule C: If hallucination_rate increases by >1.5% absolute on customer-critical slices => automatic rollback and notify safety team.

Runbook: immediate actions on regression detection:
1) Pause rollout and set traffic weight to 0 for candidate.
2) Re-run deterministic mesh replay with identical RNG seeds to confirm.
3) Run pairwise diff between baseline and candidate responses for failing slice and store sample IDs.
4) Notify owner (tagged on alert) and collect GPU/VM perf counters, kernel logs, and cache hit trace.
5) If cause is quantization (identified by increased instability in short-context samples), re-run with next-higher precision quant profile and re-evaluate.

Quantization-specific guidance:
- Always include at least one higher-precision fallback (e.g., q8_0) in the shadow mesh to isolate quant noise vs model logic changes.
- Use multi-seed aggregation to reveal nondeterministic token churn introduced by lower-precision kernels.
- Monitor KV-cache interaction: some quant kernels exhibit disproportionate instability on cold cache sequences. Include cold/warm cache perturbations explicitly.

Observability checklist (what to record):
- Request-level: request_id, slice_id, prompt_hash, seed, route, model_id, quant_profile.
- Response-level: full response, tokenization map, per-token latencies, logits (if available), KV-cache-hit boolean.
- System-level: GPU utilization, IPC, kernel choice, memory pressure, swap events.

Promotion playbook: when to roll forward fully
- Pass criteria met for 72h of continuous mesh simulation + shadow validation across all critical slices.
- No P0 regressions; all P1 triages resolved with mitigation plans.
- Cost delta within approved threshold and fallback path validated.
- Observability hooks and audit logging confirmed in Private and Dedicated deployments.

Post-promotion monitoring and stability windows:
- Post-promote stabilize window: 7 days with elevated sampling of critical customers and a shadow copy of previous baseline for 24/7 comparison.
- Run scheduled deep-eval at 24h, 72h, and 7d marks; include multi-seed aggregation and variance budgeting.

Ownership and escalation:
- Primary: model-owner (ML Engineer) — responsible for artifact and eval paper trail.
- Secondary: platform-sre — manage rollout automation and revert.
- Tertiary: applied-ml-evals — owns mesh definitions, evaluator tooling, and final acceptance.
- Escalation path: on P0 breach notify oncall -> SRE lead -> Head of Applied ML within 30 minutes.

Audit and reproducibility:
- Always store mesh-definition.yaml, eval harness seed files, and raw shadow-results in the model registry entry for the candidate model.
- Attach a minimal reproducible replay bundle to the incident ticket: includes seed set, environment digest, and exact rollout policy.

Appendix A: Example quick checklist (for on-shift engineers)
- [ ] Verify mesh-definition exists and slice weights reflect current traffic.
- [ ] Confirm evaluator suite passes smoke tests locally with baseline.
- [ ] Start mirror at 5% and validate sample distribution after first 10 minutes.
- [ ] Ensure observability streams (latency, tokens, hallucination detector) are live.
- [ ] Run summarized report and confirm no P0/P1 regressions before increasing weight.

Appendix B: FAQ
Q: How long should each rollforward window be?
A: Minimum 4 hours for low-volume routes; 12–24 hours for high-variance or customer-critical slices. Use statistical power calculation to determine sample adequacy.

Q: Can we reuse existing eval prompt sets?
A: Yes, but they must be augmented with mesh perturbations to expose cache interactions and quant instability.

Q: Is it safe to use shadow results for billing/cost estimates?
A: Only approximate—shadow runs are often sampled and may not reflect production caching/latency exactly. Use dedicated perf tests for accurate cost measurement.
